I had an AWS account that charged me like $6 per month for a year after I thought I had turned everything off. I finally went on a hunt for what was causing it, and had to escalate to support to find it.

I've gotten thousands of euro of 'free' Amazon cloud credits over the years... but the opaqueness of pricing means I won't touch it (except for S3 backups) - I just don't trust myself enough to not mess up.

Honestly I get lost inside of AWS. Only recently was I able to figure out why I was getting charged $.82/month which, in the long run, is really nothing. But it's amazing how hard it was to figure out why I was getting charged.
AWS giving you 95GB egress for free is not at all a direct answer to the insane prices... A partial direct answer that's still less free egress than almost every other free tier.

I use 500GB - 1TB per month on Cloudfront, costing about $50-100 per month, and I was going to move this over to Cloudflare... However, this AWS change will basically wipe out my entire Cloudfront bill.

I find it interesting that AWS services appear to be so tightly integrated that when there's an issue in a region, it affects most or all services. Kind of defeats the purported resiliency of cloud services.
Why after all these years is us-east-1 such a SPOF?

Consider that your typical enterprise software project will use quite a lot of these, and that you pay for them all separately, and sometimes pay twice for them (e.g. S3 you pay for storage and for outbound bandwidth).

I stopped using AWS once they hit the point where I couldn't reasonably be expected to remember what all the three letter acronyms were... every time I log into the console I find that they've removed them from my 'pinned' services.
Why does AWS use such convoluted language? Is it because they're dominant and it adds friction to moving to another provider?
